0
A Wonderful New Experience in Saigon
Oct 2014 • Friends
I just had a wonderful dinner at Noir, Dining in the Dark.

Dining in the dark is exactly what it sounds like: It's pitch black and you can't see your hand in front of your face. It's a different experience from normal dining as you can't see the food, the dining room, your companions or the wait staff. Therefore, you have to use your other senses much more and you end up focusing on things like smell, texture and of course the taste of the food.

Noir, Dining in the Dark is located in an alley off of Ha Ba Trung in an old French villa where many original features have been preserved. And it's not all in the dark: there is an upstairs dining area and an al fresco dining area on the terrace where you can have your meal in nice, soft lighting. 

Reservations are highly recommended for this restaurant so the staff can give you the whole ding in the dark experience. Upon arrival, the staff will invite you to sit in the lounge and have a mystery cocktail. All they ask is if you would like an alcoholic or non-alcoholic drink. They will also bring your group a some blindfolds and a couple games to test your sense of touch. It's a nice introduction to the dining experience later.

In the lounge, you can reconfirm your order and and special dietary requirements for anyone in your group. For dining in the dark, you only order set mystery menus. When I was there, the choices were Eastern and Western, and we all opted for the Eastern set menu.

Before heading to the darkened dining room, you have to check your phones, watches and anything else that might be able to emit light into a locker and take the key with you. As I discovered when eating, this was quite a liberating experience. 

After you're all set, the staff will introduce you to your visually impaired server who will lead you into the pitch black dining area. Our server's name was Duyen, and after our group introduced ourselves so that she knew our names, she asked us to line up single fine with our hands on the shoulders of the person in front of us. Then she led the way through a maze of black curtains into the dining area. You really can't see a thing! I was a bit disoriented trying to sit down, even though Duyen had guided me right to my chair. After everyone was seated, it felt rather cozy. The two women in our group felt a bit cold in the dining room, and Duyen brought them scarves, a remarkably nice gesture. 

Then it was time to eat! We had three courses (starter, entree and dessert), and each course was presented as several smaller dishes. For example, our starter had five things to sample, the entree had four and dessert had four. Duyen told us which order to eat each course (i.e. she told us the location of each food item on the platter) in order to enhance the overall experience. 

The food was excellent. They really put a lot of emphasis on textures and with every taste there's a whole new experience. Some items we came to a consensus on, and sometimes we'd ask Duyen if we were right or not. It was all delicious and there were a few fun surprises.

When we were all finished, Duyen helped us stand up and lined us up in the same order that we'd come in, hands on the shoulders of the person in front of us. Then she led us out, telling us to look down at the floor as we came into the light. Even the lighting was low, it was a bit overwhelming at first, but my eyes adjusted in about 30 seconds or so.

After we'd all readjusted, we were invited back to the lounge and the staff showed us pictures of what we'd just eaten. Some foods we'd nailed pretty spot on, but others were not. We'd all pretty much agreed that there was a mung bean dish in the starter course, but it turned out to be pea soup! I thought that I'd eaten an orange slice in one of my dessert dishes, but it turned out to be lemon!

Overall, it was a really nice evening with wonderful food and even nicer people. I'm looking forward to coming back soon to try the Western mystery menu.
